judged.reasons:
All five are 247-249 words, so length decided nothing. I ranked them on two things. First, does the text work as a note to a roommate? Second, does it show something real about Thea beyond a list of funeral-organist quirks?

T3 is first because it is the only one that does both. It opens on a concrete image, "I play the organ in socks, because my shoes slip on the pedals." Then it uses a real transition, "Keeping track got me in trouble in February of junior year," to move from the counting habit into the Facebook story. That story is told tightly, and T3 alone includes the detail Thea would rather hide: "I screenshotted her comment and sent it to the quiz bowl group chat to make fun of her." It also keeps her secret pleasure, "Nobody knew I liked the 63 comments, especially the mad ones." The 'permission slip' insight therefore comes after it has been earned. The roommate request ties back to that insight instead of being decoration: "If you catch me making a chart about something I'm about to leave, ask me what it's for." The roommate meets her because she left, so the request lands. Weaknesses: the opening paragraph packs in identifying facts, and "my brother calls me the Grim Reaper's DJ" feels dropped in to tick a box. The last line also garbles the notes' bigger/smaller dilemma into "makes 48 funerals bigger or just keeps me from feeling 48 separate things." The two halves are not parallel, and one side of the real dilemma is lost.

T1 is second. Every fact in it checks out against the notes, and it has the most complete line of thought: counting, the post, "My whole post was an anecdote: one church," the Census site and demography, "a permission slip with a trend line," and an honest unresolved ending. As a genre piece, though, it fails. After "Fair warning: I count things." the roommate disappears, and what follows is a supplemental essay with a salutation on top. The Duane hymn-guessing sentence sits at the end of paragraph 1 and connects to nothing. Much of the text is interview transcript stitched together almost word for word ("I think I wanted the town to be dying, because then leaving wouldn't really be leaving anybody"). That keeps the voice authentic, but the writer's own shaping is thin, and the piece ends on a quoted musing with no turn back to the reader.

T2 is the most natural roommate note. It covers socks, the $1,500 Buick, "Please don't ask me to sing. I can't.", and Arlene's all-caps texts, and it is charming. But it is a list of quirks with a single vulnerable line inserted: "sometimes I make one so I don't have to feel 48 separate things." Because the Facebook chart is never mentioned, that line has no context. It also rewrites Thea's tentative "Sometimes I think the spreadsheet is..." as a confident habit ("I've noticed"). "I like a spreadsheet more than most people do" is invented. The closer, "Maybe you'll figure it out first," is a neat little bow. The piece is pleasant but shallow next to T3 and T1.

T5 has strong borrowed voice and one consistent thread: funerals, unbelief, and the one time she cried. The Gerald Kreikemeier passage ("But that was the song. It doesn't count.") is the best single anecdote in any of the five. However, it uses none of the depth material, offers the roommate almost nothing beyond "you may as well hear it from me," and says "48 funerals" twice in 249 words. Its writerly kicker, "For someone who counts everything, I'm strict about leaving that one out," is an invented, epigram-shaped line of the kind AI drafts tend to produce. The last line, taken straight from the notes, does resonate, but the insight is implied rather than earned.

T4 is last. It reads as a grab bag: "Some things before we share a room." and then a paragraph that begins "Also:" and runs through three unrelated facts. It retells the Facebook story without Kathy, so "made me write an apology" never says who the apology was for. "I think I'm close." is left hanging, because the piece never says she doesn't know what "breathe with them" means. It also combines two separate facts into one claim: "48 funerals since June 2024 on a 1958 Wicks." "Her latest:" and "Later I realized" are small inventions. The greeting-card closer, "If you ever need someone at one, I'll sit with you.", is unsupported sentiment and is the most AI-sounding move in the set. The phone-texts framing for Arlene was a good roommate idea, but it is buried in the list.

judged.reasons:
None of the five invents statistics, studies, quotes or named sources, and none contains an outright factual error. The flagged items are generalizations stated as fact (what teachers say, how attention works, what "every school" has). T3, T4 and T5 lean on these most.

T2 ranks first because nearly every paragraph makes a point the reader hasn't heard before. Its thesis also takes a firm position: it rejects the obvious middle ground ("The common compromise, a rule against phones only during class, does not work"). It gives a real mechanism for why the compromise fails: "If a chat runs all through third period, the student who waits for the bell has a long backlog to read, so checking under the desk ... starts to look like the sensible choice." It notices that rules vary from room to room ("One teacher lets students listen to music during independent work and the next one does not, so students test the line in every class"). It sees what phones hide at lunch ("a new or shy student can spend the whole period looking at a screen while nobody notices"). It turns the self-control objection around in a new way ("They already get that practice every evening and weekend. A school day without a phone ... gives them something to measure those evenings against"). Its concessions are honest ("A dull lesson is still dull without a phone, and a student who wants to tune out can stare at the clock instead"), and it ends on a point no other text makes: the ban "has to cover teachers' phones during class too." The weakness is voice. It is impersonal and evenly polished, closer to a skilled adult than an 11th grader, and that smoothness is the main reason for the moderate AI score.

T1 is a very close second, and its voice is more human. Its observations sound like a student who has watched them happen: "some go face down on the desk and some slide into a lap under it"; "part of your attention leaves the room to guess who texted"; "it's also how you end up friends with someone who isn't already in your group chat." Its safety rebuttal has a specific twist ("during a lockdown ... a ringing phone could give away where a class is hiding"), it includes a concrete medical exception (a diabetes monitor app), and the driving-permit analogy is apt. It loses ground on structure. Paragraph 2 crams the class-only enforcement problem and the backpack point together. The opener "that says something about how much of our day phones already take up" is a little glib. The lockdown argument skips the obvious answer that a phone can be silenced. The ending repeats the enforcement point instead of building past it.

T3 has the strongest student voice ("Sometimes that student is me"; "I've sat through chemistry classes where I couldn't tell you one thing the teacher said"; "somebody would try to sneak in a second phone"). The junk-food analogy is good. Its arguments, though, are the stock set: the cafeteria of separate screens, apps engineered to be addictive, emergency panic. The opening hook asserts what "a lot of" teachers would say with no basis. The ending ("Seven hours without a phone sounds harsh. I suspect it would feel more like a relief.") is a neat, predictable turn. Its specifics are thinner than T1's or T2's.

T5 and T4 share most of their content and many whole sentences, including the cookies-on-every-desk analogy, "balancing a chemistry equation or ... Shakespeare," and "hundreds of students calling and texting at once could spread panic and rumors and drown out instructions from the adults in charge." T5 is the better of the two. It drops T4's colon title and its "not X, it's Y" closer, adds first person, and sharpens a few lines ("a minute of teaching the whole class loses, including the students who never took theirs out"; "willpower plenty of adults don't have either"). It still opens with the same hyperbolic hook ("Half the class reaches for their pockets"), and its ending is flat ("The ban I'm arguing for is limited ... So deciding on a ban is really deciding what those hours are for").

T4 is the most formulaic and the most AI-marked. It has a cliché colon title ("Phones Down, Heads Up: The Case for..."), a generic sensory hook ("Every high school student knows the sound"), and a three-part "because" thesis. Its intensifiers repeat ("quietly scrolling," "quietly shrink," "truly focus ... truly know," "should of course receive exceptions," "Parents understandably want"). Its closing antithesis is the textbook pattern ("A phone ban is not a punishment, and it is not a claim that technology is evil. It is a decision about what the school day is for"). Its claims are generic and could appear in any phone-ban essay, and it never draws on a moment of actual school experience.

One caution first: T1 and T5 are close to the same essay. Both use "like balancing a chemistry equation" with Shakespeare, the line "putting a plate of cookies on every desk and grading students on not eating them," and "hundreds of students calling and texting at once could spread panic and rumors and drown out instructions from the adults in charge," word for word. 1. T3 ranks first because it is the only essay that argues from lived school experience, which is what the brief asked for. The admission "Sometimes that student is me" pays off with "I've sat through chemistry classes where I couldn't tell you one thing the teacher said, because I spent the period half-reading a group chat." Its examples are sharp: "Rumors that might have died out by Friday get screenshotted and passed around instead." Its concession is honest: "A ban won't end cruelty, since teenagers were cruel long before smartphones existed." It ends with a real turn: "Seven hours without a phone sounds harsh. I suspect it would feel more like a relief." Weaknesses: the opening claims what "a lot of" teachers would say with no support. The candy analogy is the familiar cookies image in new clothes. The reasons are the standard set (attention, social life, cruelty, safety, self-control). The tidy line "It just happens, one glance at a time" is a little too polished.

2. T4 has the best reasoning and the tightest structure. The whole essay targets the class-only compromise, and its insights appear nowhere else. On group chats: "the student who waits for the bell has a long backlog to read, so checking under the desk ... starts to look like the sensible choice." On lunch: "anyone can leave the conversation without getting up." On passing periods: "a test grade that just posted, follows them into the next class." Its rebuttal is original: a phone-free day "gives them something to measure those evenings against." It ranks below T3 because it reads like an adult policy column, not an 11th-grader, and has no first-person stake. The ending also trails off into qualifications ("None of this makes a ban a cure. A dull lesson is still dull without a phone") rather than closing the argument.

3. T2 is concrete and sounds natural ("A lot of students would hate this rule, and I get why"). It has the best safety rebuttal of the set, "a ringing phone could give away where a class is hiding," and a fresh analogy: learn to drive "with a permit and an adult in the passenger seat before they're allowed on the highway." It ranks below T4 because the paragraphs wander. Paragraph two mixes enforcement with the backpack point. The conclusion ends on how to enforce the rule ("If teachers let some students keep a phone on the desk...") instead of why the ban matters.

4. T5 is T1 with the polish toned down. It adds "I think," puts the medical exception into the thesis, and replaces T1's slogan ending with a plainer one: "deciding on a ban is really deciding what those hours are for." The examples are still generic textbook ones (chemistry equation, Shakespeare), the cookies analogy and the "hundreds of students" sentence are still there, and it claims without support that schools have "ways to contact families quickly."

5. T1 is competent but formulaic and shows the most AI habits. Its thesis lists three reasons in a neat row ("undermine learning, weaken real friendships, and put an unfair burden"). It uses "quietly" twice ("quietly scrolling," "quietly shrink a lesson"). It ends with the "not X, it is Y" pattern ("A phone ban is not a punishment, and it is not a claim that technology is evil. It is a decision about what the school day is for") and a polished final line: "The chance to truly focus, and to truly know the classmates around them, might not be." It states a research-style finding as plain fact ("A phone breaks that attention even when it stays silent") and overgeneralizes ("every school already has phones in its offices"). There is no personal voice and no example a real student would recognize as their own.

The dated claims check out: Karikó and Weissman's 2005 paper, the 2023 Nobel Prize, the sequence released in January 2020 and the authorizations in December 2020. So the ranking comes down to hook, specificity, insight and how much filler each text uses.

T2 is first. Its opening line, "There is no virus in an mRNA vaccine, not even a dead one," is the best hook of the five, and it corrects a common misconception right away. It gives the reader a reason to care: the first response "takes a week or more while the virus multiplies," and older vaccines work by "injecting the target." Its details are the kind a teenager would remember: the spike is "the knobs on the coronavirus's surface (the 'crown' in its name)." It answers both questions readers actually ask ("Can the mRNA change your DNA? No." and "Spike alone can't give you COVID-19 either, because it carries none of the virus's genes"). The history is causal, not decoration: lab-made mRNA "set off inflammation and was destroyed too quickly," uridine was swapped, and design could start "without first growing the virus in a lab." Weaknesses: the immune paragraph lists one cell type after another, and the piece stops instead of ending.

T4 is the most precise and has the best single insight: "The vaccine has to provoke one immune reaction and avoid another." It is the only text that explains why the Nobel-winning fix mattered: "the result was inflammation and very little protein." It also has the best specific details: "three-letter chunks," "plasma cells," and "Most of these cells die once the response fades." It loses first place on fit for this reader. The opening reads like a textbook. The immune paragraph runs to eight dense sentences, with the helper-T step out of order. It skips side effects and the speed question entirely. Its voice is accurate but cool ("release the mRNA into their cytoplasm").

T1 has the most personality and suits a school blog: "Nobody sets the school on fire to practice" and "a mugshot: enough to identify the suspect, with no suspect attached." It covers lymph nodes, dendritic cells, boosters, and the honest closing line "Safety testing still takes time." But it stacks analogies and uses filler that announces importance instead of showing it ("The best part comes later." "The big advantage is speed." "Now the immune system notices something unfamiliar."). The rhetorical question "That sore arm or tired day...? That's the drill in progress." is a stock explainer move. It also has no history and no idea of why the approach was hard, so it is less specific than T2 or T4.

T5 shares whole sentences with T3, for example "Some copies are displayed on the cell's surface; others are released and picked up by immune cells" and "cells have no normal way to turn it into DNA." It improves on T3 in two ways. It asks the right question, "How can one protein protect you from a whole virus?", and it adds real dates ("shared in January 2020 ... authorized that December"). But the opening is the same generic one ("deals quickly with germs it has met before"), the immune paragraph is a list, and the last paragraph crams speed, decades of research and the Nobel into one block. It also overstates the uridine result ("kept lab-made mRNA from setting off inflammation").

"like a key cut for one lock" is the stock lock-and-key analogy. "Most importantly" is a filler signpost. "The big idea:" opens a summary built on three parallel clauses that ends in the cliché "ready when it counts." Its history line, "studying mRNA technology for decades," is the vaguest of the five, and it leaves out dendritic cells, lymph nodes and every name and date.

I checked the facts in all five. None has an invented statistic, quote or study. The dates used are all correct: the virus genome was shared in January 2020, the first vaccines were authorized in December 2020, Karikó and Weissman published in 2005, and they won the Nobel Prize in 2023. "Since the 1990s" is also correct. So the ranking comes down to precision, depth and how well each one works for a high-school science club reader.

T5 (1st) covers the most ground in about 447 words without padding. It opens with a concrete hook: "There is no virus in an mRNA vaccine, not even a dead one. The syringe holds a strand of genetic instructions wrapped in fat." It is more exact than the others on timing, saying a first response "takes a week or more while the virus multiplies," where T1 and T4 say only "days." It adds a fact students will like: the spike is "the knobs on the coronavirus's surface (the \"crown\" in its name)." It explains selection ("B cells whose receptors fit spike multiply"), the DNA myth, side effects, why the vaccines were fast, and the uridine fix, all in plain language. Its weak spots are the loose phrase "the vaccine is mostly a genetic sequence" and the stock pattern "Can the mRNA change your DNA? No."

T3 (2nd) is the most precise science of the five, with codons ("three-letter chunks"), plasma cells and the contraction phase ("Most of these cells die once the response fades, but memory B and T cells stay behind"). Its last paragraph has the best idea in any of the texts: "The vaccine has to provoke one immune reaction and avoid another." It explains why unmodified mRNA failed ("inflammation and very little protein") and adds the correct detail "Both COVID-19 mRNA vaccines use a modified uridine." It ranks below T5 because the voice is textbook-dry, there is no hook or wrap-up, and it never says why the vaccines could be made so fast.

T1 (3rd) is clean and correct. It asks the best student-level question in any of the texts: "How can one protein protect you from a whole virus?" It also includes the real timeline and the Nobel Prize. However, it overstates the Karikó/Weissman result ("kept lab-made mRNA from setting off inflammation") and is vague on the cell biology ("others are released and picked up by immune cells"). Many of its sentences are almost word-for-word the same as T4's ("short-lived molecule called messenger RNA," "Some copies are displayed on the cell's surface; others are released and picked up by immune cells," "cells have no normal way to turn it into DNA"). It is the stronger of the two.

T2 (4th) has the liveliest classroom voice. Its fire-drill frame holds together ("That's the drill in progress," "the practice sometimes needs an update"), and the mugshot line is good: "enough to identify the suspect, with no suspect attached." Its mechanism paragraph is correct and fairly full (dendritic cells, lymph nodes, helper T cells, "Y-shaped proteins"). It also adds two useful points: boosters, and "Safety testing still takes time." But it has no names, dates or history, says "A spike protein on its own can't make you sick" when it means "can't cause an infection," and leans on blog filler ("The best part comes later," "The big advantage is speed").

T4 (5th) is the most generic and template-like. It promises "a particularly clever way" and then uses stock signposts: "Start with what mRNA is," "Now the training begins," "Most importantly," two rhetorical-question headers, and a closing summary that starts "The big idea:". It has the fewest specifics (no names, dates or dendritic cells), and it includes two inaccuracies: "contains only these instructions" and the comparison "like the cell's own messages," since a cell's natural mRNAs break down faster than the modified vaccine mRNA.

T4 (3rd) is tight and finished. It has a strong title and some well-judged lines. Its best insight, "'Colossal' is a strange word for something that was 'minute' four chapters earlier. All five essays share one skeleton. Each opens on a grade that doesn't match what the student knows, then argues that a grade should show current understanding (all five use a chemistry/stoichiometry example). Each says retakes change what students do with a returned test, answers the "makes students lazy" objection with conditions, offers the driving test for "real life has no second chances," and covers the cost to teachers. Since the bones are the same, the ranking turns on what each writer adds to them. None of the five invents a statistic, study, named source or quote. The hypothetical scores in T3 (58/88/73) are an illustration, and the arithmetic is right. The flagged lines are unargued generalizations, not made-up facts. Several texts make the same unproven claim that corrections plus a retake are "more work than studying the first time."

T3 (best) is the only one that commits to a specific, arguable policy: "the new score replacing the old one instead of being averaged with it." It then proves the point with a worked case: "If it averages the two scores, her report card shows a 73. Both numbers are weighed down by a confusion she has already cleared up." Its cumulative-subject paragraph names real dependencies ("A student who never learned to factor will struggle when the class reaches quadratic equations"). It also explains why students skip review: "the sensible choice is to move on and hope the gap stays hidden. In a cumulative subject, it rarely does." The laziness rebuttal goes further than the others: "she learns it a few weeks after her classmates do." The teacher-cost line is the best sentence in the set: "a good reason to limit the policy and a weak reason to refuse it." Weaknesses: the voice is adult and impersonal with no student presence. The fairness and real-world objections are crammed into one paragraph. The ending stops on policy details ("which is the behavior a grading system should reward") instead of closing the argument.

T5 is close behind. It has two moves no other text makes. First, the curve point: "Unless the class is graded on a curve, one student's grade doesn't take anything away from another's." It is clever but ignores class rank. Second, a real limit on its own position: "I wouldn't extend this to final exams... there's no next unit." Its concrete details sound like real school life ("a history test and a chemistry test on the same day," "explain in writing why the right answer is right," "anyone who never figured out unit three walks into unit four already behind"). The SAT example is accurate and fits better than T1's "writers revise." The voice is a natural first-person student, with human hedges like "maybe the questions they missed." It has no hook or title, and the finals limit arrives late, in the conclusion. Its closing sentence still lands.

T2 has the strongest teen voice and the most emotional appeal. The fairness paragraph is vivid ("Others work evening shifts or watch younger siblings until midnight," "A kid whose family was falling apart for a week"). The October/November contrast works. It leans on crafted devices, though: "Every student knows the feeling," "The main reason is simple," the rhetorical "Isn't that the whole point of school?", and a tidy callback ending ("the next time I flip a test over"). It shifts between "does not" and "there's." "One rough test can pull a semester grade down a full letter" is a quantitative claim with no qualification.

Accuracy check first. All five get the core physics right: sunlight is a mix of colors, N2/O2 molecules are much smaller than visible wavelengths, scattering goes as 1/wavelength^4, and the sunset light path is long. The numbers T1, T3 and T4 give are correct: (700/450)^4 is about 5.9, so "about six times" (T1) and "almost six times" (T3) hold, and "dozens of times more air" at the horizon matches an air mass of about 38. Rayleigh 1871 and Krakatoa 1883 are real (pedantic note: in 1871 he was still J. W. Strutt; the title came in 1873). None of the texts invents statistics, studies or quotes. T4's Apollo and NASA-rover references are real, well-known facts, not made-up sources.

T1 (best): It states its thesis up front ("what changes is how much air the light passes through"), and each paragraph does one job. It defines nanometers, turns the law into something you can picture ("Halve the wavelength and you get 16 times the scattering"), and has the clearest violet passage ("triggers the color-sensing cells in your eyes in a ratio your brain reads as pale blue"). It is the only text with a single principle linking clouds and smoke: "their size decides which colors get scattered most". Its experiment ending is the best teaching in the set because the reader changes one variable and it maps onto path length: "Stir in more milk and the beam gets redder, as the Sun does when its light crosses more air." Weaknesses: "1 divided by the wavelength to the fourth power" is clunky. The volcanic-particle claim is oversimplified: post-Krakatoa aerosols were near-wavelength in size, which is why blue and green suns were also reported. The voice is clean but plain.

T4 (close second): It has the most interesting content. The Moon as a control case ("Apollo astronauts saw a black sky in full daylight"), Mars as the reverse case ("NASA rovers have photographed Martian sunsets with a blue glow around the sun"), and the parenthetical "it is lighting up the afternoon sky for people farther west" (simplified geometry, but defensible) all build understanding rather than just decorate. A science-club reader would remember this one. It drops below T1 on structure. It opens straight into "Sunlight looks white" with no observed scene, and nanometers go undefined. The clouds/Krakatoa paragraph is a grab-bag ("Smoke and volcanic ash can make sunsets a deeper red" gives no mechanism). The experiment is never explained and ends flatly on "its light looks orange."

T3 (third): It is nearly a twin of T1 and equally accurate. Some lines are strong: "its blue is sprayed across the sky while most of the red goes straight on", "even the part opposite the sun", "Violet scatters even more, and the sky does contain some", and it explains the experiment ("tiny milk particles scatter blue more than red"). The prose is clumsier: "spreads it into a rainbow because it is every color mixed". The cloud-droplet sentence is stuck onto the end of the Krakatoa paragraph. The sentence "Both colors come from the air scattering sunlight, and what changes is..." uses the same frame as T1 but less crisply.

T2 (fourth): It has the most personality: the title "(and Why Sunsets Aren't)", the clipped "Three things work against it.", and a nice observation that leftover light "hits the undersides of clouds". It also teaches a misconception: "bounced from molecule to molecule" suggests multiple scattering, when sky blue is mostly single scattering. It repeats the doubtful line about violet "absorbed high in the atmosphere" (ozone absorbs UV, and its visible band is in the orange). Signposting tells: "Start with the light itself.", "Now the sunset.", "The rule that matters here is simple:". The closing line "You've just made a sky and a sunset in a cup" is stock.

It has the most believable student voice ("The word that bothers me is 'tedious.'", "which I find colder than anything she said"), and it adds a real qualification: "He takes on her calm but never her belief that the blood washes off." That leads to a causal claim the others don't make: "that's why the guilt breaks her and doesn't stop him: she's the one who expected it to be easy." Its "prose instead of verse" point is supported by how the quotes file formats Q4. The plain title ("Blood on the Hands in Macbeth") and the absolute "never claims" cost it a little.

T1 delivers on its opening promise ("down to the words they use"). "'How easy is it then!' has become 'Oh, oh, oh!', an exclamation with no words left in it" is a sharp line. But the last paragraph is overloaded, and the conclusion rests on speculation ("awake she was probably still forcing it down") and on a point outside the file ("his ending is the worse one").

T5 is accurate and well organized ("She flips the moral meaning of color"), but it reads like a polished model answer. It leans on stock evaluative words ("The word 'tedious' is chilling because it is so flat") and ends on a neat chiasmus ("The one who said guilt could be rinsed away cannot rinse it...") rather than a claim of its own. It has no personal voice, and its smoothness makes it the most likely of the five to be machine-written.

T4 comes last. It invents staging ("Macbeth stares at his hand", "sees the same thing and shrugs", "ghost ruins the banquet") and leans on clichés ("you have the whole play in miniature"). Its conclusion contradicts its own argument: it says Macbeth "put down" the horror and has "stopped trying to get clean", then generalizes that guilt "doesn't go away". The essay never squares that with Macbeth's case.

judged.reasons:
All five texts are three paragraphs of 469 to 499 words. All five use the same skeleton: scaffold, then "Able," then the forest, then the Conclusion. All of them quote only Q1 to Q4, and the quotes are accurate. What separates them is the quality of the argument and the close reading, plus a few factual slips.

T2 (1st) is the only text with a thesis that is arguable and runs through the whole piece: "at each stage Hawthorne defines it through the people looking at it." It tests that claim against the evidence. It catches the attribution in "They said." It admits that Ch. XVIII "breaks the pattern by showing the letter from Hester's side." It finds the audience again even in the ending: "sorrow, awe and reverence are what onlookers feel, and the letter is still 'looked upon.'" That builds to a real payoff: "Hester decides to wear it, but other people still decide what it means." The "resumed" observation is also correct, since the word appears on both sides of the clause in Q4. Its one real error is "the first decision about the letter that Hester makes herself." Unclasping the letter in the forest and throwing it aside was her own decision too, and T2 contradicts itself in its own last lines: "In the forest, freedom meant throwing the letter aside." "A spell is cast from outside ... done to Hester by the people who read it" stretches Q1. The prose is controlled and sometimes heavy on signposting ("sets the pattern," "The last stage begins"), but it is not formulaic.

T3 (2nd) has the sharpest small observations of the five. On the Ch. XIII line it writes: "'Refused' shows that the old meaning is still there. People have to push against it, and only 'many' of them manage to, not all." On chronology it writes: "Five chapters after 'Able,' the narrator still calls the letter a stigma," and the chapter count is right. On word order it writes: "Sorrow comes first, and reverence comes last, tacked on with 'yet' and 'too.'" The voice sounds like a believable strong student ("an odd phrase for an embroidered letter until you think about what a spell does"). It falls short of T2 on structure. The thesis is tacked onto the end of paragraph 1, and the essay never shows why the last change is "the bigger" one. It overstates one contrast: "in Chapter XIII it was only what 'many people' said." In Q2 the narrator says in his own voice that "The letter was the symbol of her calling." "The town gives the letter a kinder name" also clashes with its own later point that only "many" people did.

T1 (3rd) is accurate and has one original move: "When people renamed it Able, they swapped one word for another. Here Hawthorne gives no single word, only 'something'." It then reads "something" as Hester's whole history, which a teacher would reward. The weaknesses are mostly structural. Paragraph 1 combines the thesis with the scaffold reading. "The bigger one" and then "The bigger change" repeat the claim instead of developing it. Some readings are thinner than T3's: "refused" is glossed only as "something people chose." "That doesn't make it a plain badge of honor" is the same stock phrase T5 uses.

T4 (4th) is competent but mostly summary. It quotes long blocks, including nearly all of the Q4 sentence and all of Q2, and comments on them only briefly. It uses filler tells: "That last phrase matters." "Then comes the line I find most revealing." The ending has a tidy tricolon ("from a sentence handed down by the town, to a word the town rewrites, to a symbol Hester picks up") and a neat closing aphorism. "brands Hester Prynne as a sinner" and "the authorities of Boston" come from outside the quotes file. "Hester has helped so many people that 'The letter was the symbol of her calling'" reverses the order of Q2, which states the symbol first and gives the helpfulness as the explanation, and it leaves a capital T in the middle of the sentence. "Reverence is a long way from the spell of the market-place" is its best line.

T5 (5th) reads the most like a template. It has a title, and it leans on not-X-but-Y frames ("less as a label than as a wall," "not only public shame but isolation," "belong to artwork and decoration, not to punishment," "no longer a sentence handed down to her but a choice") and stock lines ("Yet Hawthorne complicates this from the start," "Hawthorne is careful here"). It ends on a grand tricolon. Its closing claim is wrong: "the magistrates who made the letter could control its shape." The quotes file never says the magistrates made the letter (in the novel, Hester embroiders it herself). The claim also contradicts T5's own paragraph 1, which says the embroidery was "more than the authorities intended," and that intent is itself unsupported. "This is the most important shift in the novel" is asserted, not argued. Its close reading of "embroidered"/"illuminated" and "stitched into the fabric" is decent, but it adds nothing T1 doesn't already do more plainly.

judged.reasons:
All five follow the same route through Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4, and every one makes the point that Q3 shows Hester still felt the letter as shame after the town started calling it "Able." So the ranking comes down to three things: what each writer adds beyond that shared reading, whether the claims hold up, and how much the voice sounds like a student.

T5 is first. It has the most original analysis, in its last paragraph. First it sets the forest scene against the ending: "In the forest, the stigma left only when the letter came off... At the end it's the other way around. The letter stays on... it 'ceased to be a stigma.'" Then it reads the wording closely: "When people renamed it Able, they swapped one word for another. Here Hawthorne gives no single word, only 'something.'" The thesis is clear and comes first ("I think the last change, when the choice becomes Hester's, is the bigger one"), and the essay argues it. The voice sounds like a capable student ("That's a strange way to describe a punishment"). Its only flaw is the spliced quote "the symbol of 'so dark a tale.'" The close reading of "embroidered"/"illuminated" also appears in T2 and T3, so it is less fresh.

T4 is second. It has the sharpest small-scale close reading: "'Refused' shows that the old meaning is still there... only 'many' of them manage to, not all"; "Five chapters after 'Able,' the narrator still calls the letter a stigma"; "He uses 'resumed' twice"; "Sorrow comes first, and reverence comes last, tacked on with 'yet' and 'too.'" The plain voice fits the class best ("until you think about what a spell does: it works on you whether you agree to it or not"). It falls behind T5 for two reasons. Its narrator-versus-"many people" contrast leaves out the narrator's own line in Q2, "The letter was the symbol of her calling." And its last sentence is flat and summarizing.

T1 is third. It has the most unified argument: the A is always "defined... through the people looking at it." It handles the forest scene, which breaks that pattern, well, and it ends on a real twist: "Hester decides to wear it, but other people still decide what it means." But the central claim about agency has a slip. "The first decision about the letter that Hester makes herself" ignores her throwing the letter aside in Ch. XVIII, which the essay itself described one paragraph earlier. "A spell is cast from outside... by the people who read it" pushes Q1 further than it goes. The prose is dense and reads like an adult. Phrasing such as "sets the pattern" and "breaks the pattern" feels practiced, not like a student's.

T3 is fourth. It is polished and has good moments ("less as a label than as a wall"; "never stitched into the fabric in the first place"). But its closing line is wrong and contradicts the essay itself: "the magistrates who made the letter could control its shape." Nothing in the quotes file supports this. It also clashes with the essay's own first paragraph, which says the embroidery already exceeded "what the authorities intended." It reads like a template: a "not X but Y" frame used over and over ("not only public shame but isolation," "no longer a sentence handed down to her but a choice," "does not turn into a simple badge of honor"), stock moves like "Hawthorne complicates this from the start" and "Hawthorne is careful here," and a neat triad at the end, "from spell to calling to chosen symbol."

T2 is last. It retells and quotes more than it analyzes, often dropping in a whole quote with little comment. Its opening claims ("authorities of Boston," "brands Hester Prynne as a sinner") are not in the quotes file. It uses filler signposts: "That last phrase matters." "Then comes the line I find most revealing." It overclaims that the ending is "where the meaning finally becomes hers," even though its own evidence describes how onlookers feel. It also closes on a stock triad: "from a sentence handed down by the town, to a word the town rewrites, to a symbol Hester picks up again by choice." The best line, "Reverence is a long way from the spell of the market-place," does not make up for the thin analysis.
